A denomination is an organized, official branch or sub-group within a religion. Religions like Christianity are not one single unified group — they are split into many distinct branches, each with its own specific beliefs, rules, rituals, leadership structure, and traditions.

For example, within Christianity, the major denominations include:

  • Catholic
  • Baptist
  • Methodist
  • Lutheran
  • Presbyterian
  • Anglican
  • Pentecostal
  • Eastern Orthodox

Each of these is a denomination — a specific, named, organized version of Christianity. They all believe in Jesus Christ and the Bible at a broad level, but they differ from each other in important ways: how they worship, how their churches are governed, which rituals they practice, and what specific doctrines (teachings) they emphasize.

Other religions have this too. In Islam, the main denominations are Sunni and Shia. In Judaism, there are Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform. Even Buddhism and Hinduism have their own distinct branches.

Nondenominational means not belonging to, not affiliated with, and not restricted to any specific denomination.

Something that is nondenominational does not take sides among religious denominations. It does not follow the specific rules, doctrines, or identity of any one branch. It is open to everyone — regardless of which denomination they belong to, or even if they belong to none.

Think of it this way: if denominations are different clubs within the same broad religion, something nondenominational is not a member of any club. It stands outside all of them, welcoming everyone equally.
Where you'll see this word used

1. Nondenominational church
This is by far the most common use. A nondenominational church is a Christian church that does not officially identify itself as Catholic, Baptist, Methodist, or any other denomination. It may draw from the teachings of various Christian traditions, but it is not formally governed by, or accountable to, any denomination's national or international body.

Someone might choose a nondenominational church because they find the rules and structure of traditional denominations too rigid, or because they want a faith community that doesn't emphasize denominational divisions.

Important note: A nondenominational church is still a religious institution. It still believes in God and Jesus. "Nondenominational" does NOT mean non-religious or atheist. It just means the church is not stamped with a denominational label.

2. Nondenominational ceremony or service
A nondenominational wedding, funeral, or prayer service is one that is deliberately designed to be accessible and respectful to people from any religious background — or no religious background. No one feels excluded because the ceremony is not tied to the specific rituals of any one religion.

For example: Two people from different religious backgrounds (say, one Hindu and one Christian) might choose a nondenominational wedding ceremony so that both families feel comfortable and included.

3. Nondenominational chapel or prayer room
You'll often find these in hospitals, airports, universities, and military bases. These are quiet spaces for reflection and prayer that are not dedicated to any specific religion. A Muslim, a Christian, a Jew, and a person with no religious belief can all use the same room, because it belongs to no denomination and excludes no one.

4. Nondenominational school or organization
A nondenominational school does not promote the doctrines of any particular religion. A nondenominational charity helps people regardless of their religious identity.
The single most important idea behind this word

The heart of "nondenominational" is neutrality and inclusivity across religious divisions. It signals that something has deliberately chosen not to align itself with the beliefs, rules, or identity of any specific religious sub-group, so that it can serve, welcome, or represent everyone.
A subtle but important distinction: nondenominational vs. interdenominational

These two words look similar but mean different things.

  • Interdenominational means involving multiple denominations working together. For example, an interdenominational prayer service might have a Catholic priest, a Baptist minister, and a Methodist pastor all participating together. The denominations are still present — they are just cooperating.
  • Nondenominational means not belonging to any denomination at all. No denomination is present in an official sense. It exists completely outside the denominational structure.

So: interdenominational = multiple denominations coming together; nondenominational = no denomination at all.
A subtle but important distinction: nondenominational vs. secular

• Secular means entirely without religion — not religious at all.
  • Nondenominational can still be religious (and often is). It simply means the religious content or institution does not belong to a specific denomination.

A nondenominational chapel is still a place for religious reflection. A secular building is just a building with no religious purpose whatsoever.

• "After years in a strict Catholic school, she felt more comfortable attending a nondenominational church where no single tradition dominated."
  • "The couple held a nondenominational ceremony at a garden so that guests from all faiths could feel equally welcome."
  • "The hospital's nondenominational prayer room is available to patients of every religion, as well as those with none."
  • "The charity was nondenominational, meaning it provided aid to communities without regard for their religious beliefs."
  • "The university's chapel is nondenominational — it hosts Christian services on Sunday, Jewish Shabbat on Friday, and meditation sessions on weekday mornings."

Nondenominational describes something — a church, ceremony, space, or organization — that is not tied to or defined by any particular religious denomination, making it open to and inclusive of people from all religious backgrounds, or none at all.
